expected_evidence: geological: anomalous platinum (and often associated iridium/nickel) enrichment in a discrete sediment layer at ~10,950 BCE (Younger Dryas onset 'boundary layer'), detectable via ICP-MS in lake cores, peat bogs, loess sections
geological: co-occurring proxies often invoked with impact-ejecta claims — microspherules, nanodiamonds, meltglass, magnetic spherules, a 'black mat' horizon
astronomical: crater search / impact-structure candidates, cosmic-dust/extraterrestrial-isotope signatures (He-3, Ir ratios) consistent with bolide airburst or impact
material: archaeological-context correlations (Clovis-era site abandonment layers, faunal turnover) at Mexican sites bracketing the same date
genetic: megafaunal population bottleneck/extinction signals dated near 10,950 BCE (weak, indirect corroboration)

model-prior: general Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature reporting platinum anomalies at multiple global sites, including some Mexican lake-sediment cores (e.g., Lake Cuitzeo-type studies) — recalled from training, not independently verified here
response.rationale: The interval -10950 (~10,950 BCE) sits essentially at the Younger Dryas onset, so the 'younger-dryas' detectability row is the correct reference rather than an unspecified period. The claim hinges almost entirely on geological (sediment/ice-core geochemistry) and secondarily astronomical evidence types, which have the highest detectability scores in this period (geological 0.65, astronomical 0.70) — platinum is chemically robust and well-preserved in stratified sediments/ice over 13,000 years, and such YD-boundary platinum anomalies have genuinely been reported in the literature at multiple sites worldwide (a fact I recall from training as model-prior, unverified in this session). Material, genetic, linguistic, textual, oral_tradition, and iconographic channels are largely irrelevant or near-zero for a geochemical signature this ancient and are not expected to contribute much. Given the relatively favorable geological/astronomical detectability for this period, absence of confirmed evidence would not be strongly excused by low detectability — if the anomaly exists at the claimed Mexican location, it is plausible it could have been sampled and reported already; conversely, existing literature on this specific hypothesis is contested (the broader Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis remains scientifically debated, with several failed replication attempts), so a lack of independent corroboration should carry meaningful evidentiary weight against the hypothesis, not be dismissed purely as a detection-limit problem. I set the adjustment slightly above the raw geological/astronomical average (~0.55) to reflect that platinum-anomaly detection is a mature, well-established technique in this specific sub-domain, making practical detectability somewhat better than the generic table value for the period as a whole.
